Neonates of the bulb mite, Rhizoglyphus robini, emerge from the egg at a total length of approximately 0.0167 cm [Lb = approximately 0.0167 cm] and a volume of 1.49 × 10⁻⁶ cm³ , reflecting the modest size typical of astigmatid larvae. These initial dimensions are derived from volumetric calculations based on the formula for an ellipsoid and represent the earliest measurable stage of the post-embryonic life cycle. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the duration of the egg stage is remarkably brief, with hatching occurring 2.86 days [ab = 2.86 days] after oviposition. This rapid embryonic development, recorded at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], is consistent with the high developmental rates observed among closely related acarid mites occupying ephemeral, nutrient-rich microhabitats. The protonymph that emerges is immediately capable of locomotion and commences exogenous feeding without a prolonged period of yolk dependency, a life-history trait that facilitates rapid colonization of newly available food patches such as decomposing organic matter and fungal colonies.

A second cohort of neonate bulb mites was measured to have a slightly larger total length at birth, averaging 0.0169 cm [Lb = 0.0169 cm], with a corresponding body volume of 1.74 × 10⁻⁶ cm³ . This minor variation in neonatal dimensions likely reflects differences in maternal provisioning or egg size among the founding females in the experimental colony. When reared exclusive on a diet of yeast at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the emergence from the egg took 2.58 days [ab = 2.58 days]. It must be noted that this age upon ecdysis could be off by a maximum of one day, as the larvae were not inspected during the night for emerging from the egg. Such short developmental times at 27 °C underscore the mite's high intrinsic growth potential, a characteristic that allows it to exploit transient resources before competitors or predators become established.

Sexual maturation, or the attainment of puberty, in Rhizoglyphus robini is accompanied by marked changes in body size. Under laboratory rearing at 27 °C, the total length at puberty has been recorded as 0.034 cm [Lp = 0.034 cm], while the corresponding volume at puberty is 1.17 × 10⁻⁵ cm³ . This size represents a substantial increase from the neonatal stage, reflecting the cumulative effects of several molts and active feeding during the deutonymphal phase. The time since birth at which puberty is reached is 32.94 days [tp = 32.94 days] when measured at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period, relative to the brief egg stage, is thought to be necessary for the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves and the development of the reproductive organs. In contrast, a separate cohort of mites reared under slightly different nutritional conditions reached puberty at a smaller length of 0.054 cm [Lp = 0.054 cm] and a larger volume of 5.09 × 10⁻⁵ cm³ , suggesting a trade-off between somatic growth and the timing of reproductive competence. For these individuals, the time since birth at puberty was much shorter, at just 9.58 days [tp = 9.58 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], indicating that resource availability can strongly influence the pace of developmental milestones.

The ultimate total length attained by fully mature adult bulb mites has been documented to reach up to 0.0486 cm [Li = up to 0.0486 cm], with an associated ultimate volume of 3.54 × 10⁻⁵ cm³ , representing the asymptotic body size in typical laboratory cultures. However, when provided with an exceptionally rich diet and low population density, some individuals have been recorded achieving an even greater ultimate total length of 0.0674 cm [Li = 0.0674 cm] and an ultimate volume of 0.0001 cm³ . These maximum recorded dimensions are likely near the physiological upper limit for this species, constrained by the mechanics of the cuticle and the efficiency of the tracheal respiratory system. At the standard rearing temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum reproductive output observed for females in this species shows considerable variation. One group of breeders attained a daily rate of 2.65 eggs per day [Ri = 2.65 eggs per day] when maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], whereas a particularly fecund lineage produced as many as 21.89 eggs per day [Ri = 21.89 eggs per day] under the same thermal conditions, highlighting the substantial intraspecific genetic or maternal-effect variance in reproductive potential.

Longevity data for Rhizoglyphus robini, recorded under constant conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], indicate an average lifespan of 69.76 days [am = 69.76 days] in the laboratory, though this figure can be influenced by feeding regime and population density. In a separate captive experiment, a shorter average lifespan of 40.38 days [am = 40.38 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] was observed, likely due to a higher metabolic cost associated with elevated fecundity in that particular cohort. Despite these differences, the species exhibits a classic r-selected life-history strategy, with rapid development, early reproduction, and high fecundity compensating for relatively short adult survival. Under natural conditions, where mites face desiccation risk, predation by predatory mesostigmatids, and fluctuating food availability, realized lifespans in the field are expected to be considerably lower than these laboratory maxima. Future comparative studies between populations from different geographic origins would help clarify the extent to which these demographic traits are plastic versus genetically canalized.
